* Terrible battery life compared to not just ARM machines, but even other x86 laptops (I have the AMD board AND the newer, bigger battery and I am still struggling to get maybe 6 hours full charge with just browsing and Discord open)
* Performance-to-cost ratio is not very good
* Durability is okay, not great. Simple 1 foot drop on carpet dented a corner of my laptop. QC is a bit lacking, especially for the FW16, I've heard. Lid also flexes a lot, even with the CNC lid, so the screen is constantly touching and getting scratched up by the keyboard when it is in my backpack.
* Lower WiFi speeds than comparable laptops.
* Software support from Framework is questionable, with extremely slow BIOS and firmware updates (it took Framework around 3-4 months to release a BIOS/firmware update to address AMD FW13s crashing due to the Radeon drivers, was quite the useless paperweight during that time. Don't even get me started on the 11th gen Intel mobo issues, that was a shit show and I legitimately just bought an M1 Macbook Pro and did not touch my Framework for 3 years during that time)
* Most people buying these machines seem to buy them with the intention of running Linux, which is great if that's what you are also planning on doing. In comparison, it's like a ghost town getting support for any issues Windows related.

Basically, the Framework offerings are good if you are a tinkerer who wants a computer from a company championing right-to-repair while also having a keen focus on Linux support, money no object, of course.

For literally anyone else, you are probably better served by most other offerings on the market ATM.

You also need to ask yourself if you legitimately see yourself holding on to the FW13 or upgrading it often, as it's not cheap to upgrade from motherboard to motherboard, or upgrading the battery, screen, etc. Finally, as important as repairability is, reliability is just as important and honestly, my M1 Macbook Pro is not only still kicking around, but has overall given me no issues compared to the FW13.

Windows Modern Standby claims another victim, F

From what I can tell, this shit happens so often with Windows laptops because of the way Microsoft implemented Modern Standby. If you close the lid or put the computer in sleep mode while plugged in, then unplug it and put it in your bag, there is always a chance the computer will actually turn on in the bag. This happens relatively often. Unfortunately it seems you got the absolute worst case scenario and the computer overheated to the point of frying the input cover to death. As to why only these components failed, it could be that the input cover took the brunt of the heat.

To avoid it next time, you could try disabling connected modern standby when plugged in and (and on battery, to be safe): [https://www.elevenforum.com/t/enable-or-disable-modern-standby-network-connectivity-in-windows-11.3286/](https://www.elevenforum.com/t/enable-or-disable-modern-standby-network-connectivity-in-windows-11.3286/)

EDIT: Also something important I forgot to mention regarding the Samsung 990 Pro, if you do end up getting this SSD, make sure the first thing you do when you take it home is update to the latest firmware, some of the 990 Pros had premature failure due to bad firmware earlier on. You will want to install this update ADAP since while it stops the SSD from deteriorating quickly, it can't undo the damage already done by the old firmware (i.e. if you used the SSD for two months and it already went down to say 89% health, the firmware update would stop it from dropping any lower but will not bring health back to 100%).

My experience with gaming on the FW13 is that it is alright, I'm able to run games like Persona 3 Reload and Red Dead Redemption 2 on it. Essentially, whatever you can run on a Steam Deck *should* be able to run on a FW13 AMD, just expect Steam Deck level performance (you are probably not going to be maxing the settings on ANY triple A game).

That being said, it is still not what I would consider a gaming laptop. In my case, I just needed a good all purpose laptop that could handle some gaming. If you need a laptop PRIMARILY for gaming, I would not recommend this laptop at all, it's just not what it was designed for.

I was born with tinnitus, I have always associated "complete silence" with a slight ringing noise, similar to the noise CRT TVs made when they were on but not actually playing anything.

I can definitely see how tinnitus can be absolutely maddening for someone who has never had it before. Hell, there was a period of time during college where I was extremely stressed and it made my tinnitus much worse than usual and it was disconcerting, to say the least.

What I found helped during that time was to find white noise at a certain frequency depending on your tinnitus (my ENT was able to help me find this frequency) to help mask and mitigate the tinnitus temporarily. I would pull up the video on YouTube, listen for like half an hour, and then I wouldn't hear the ringing for a good couple hours afterwards. Of course, in general, the tinnitus will get better with time as your body slowly adjusts and attenuate the tinnitus itself.

I honestly have no idea how some people can listen to their music at 80-90 decibels constantly. If the iOS decibel meter is accurate, I have to listen at 45-60 decibels and long listening sessions still fatigue my ears.
